solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: What gets water inside? Employ scheme when it’s baking outside (10)

indicatorNotes.outside: Something outside a thing surrounds it, so HOT wraps round the other pieces.

annotation.surface: A gardener's riddle about watering in hot weather.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition reads like a question about rain or plumbing; it is a playful description of a potted plant kept indoors.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: potted greenery kept indoors is watered by its owner in the living room, not by rain in the garden.

entries.clue: Outstanding triumph in uphill advance (5)

indicatorNotes.in: One thing placed in another sits inside it, so WIN goes inside the reversed GO.
indicatorNotes.uphill: In a down entry, going uphill means reading from the bottom upwards, so GO becomes OG.

annotation.surface: A climber's victory while pushing up a slope.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise for the triumph, but here it means still unpaid.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the money sense: a bill not yet settled is still due to be paid.

entries.clue: Allowance of three points (7)

annotation.surface: A modest allowance measured in points.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Three points' asks for three different kinds of point: a compass point, a pointed tip and an end point.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fixed regular sum paid to a clergyman, student or trainee to live on.

entries.clue: Animal regularly appearing in spring (3)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Something done regularly happens at even intervals, so take letters at even steps: every other one.
indicatorNotes.appearing in: What appears in a word is already there on show, so the letters come from inside 'spring'.

blocks.note: sPrInG: second, fourth and sixth letters

annotation.surface: An animal that shows up every spring.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spring' sets the scene for lambs and chicks, but it is only the source of the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the farmyard porker is one example of an animal.

entries.clue: Army equipment badly blocking main road (9)

indicatorNotes.blocking: An obstacle blocking a road sits in the middle of it, so ILL goes inside ARTERY.

blocks.note: an artery is a main road

annotation.surface: Military vehicles have broken down across a highway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Badly' looks like it describes the blocking, but it is the piece that does the blocking.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: heavy guns such as cannon and howitzers, the kit a gunnery regiment fights with.

entries.clue: Clock, say, showing minutes in order (5)

indicatorNotes.in: Something put in a container sits inside it, so M goes inside TIER.

blocks.note: a tier is a rank or order

annotation.surface: A clock with its minutes set out in sequence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In order' reads as a phrase meaning correctly arranged; split it, and 'in' puts M inside 'order', a tier.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'say': a clock is one device that measures elapsed time, like a stopwatch or kitchen gadget.

entries.clue: Concert pianist extremely quick to respond (6)

indicatorNotes.extremely: The extremes of a word are its two ends, so take only its first and last letters.

blocks.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as at the BBC Proms

annotation.surface: A concert pianist who reacts fast.
annotation.walkthrough: The Proms are a famous summer season of classical concerts in London, so PROM is a concert.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone punctual and on the ball acts without delay when asked.

entries.clue: Complaining after church has gone very cold (6)

indicatorNotes.has gone: Something that has gone is no longer there, so CH is removed from the word.

blocks.note: ch = church; it is taken out

annotation.surface: Someone grumbling after the service because the church is freezing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'After' is part of the surface story: the grumbling carries on once the church has gone from it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from weather talk: wind or frost so harsh it seems to nip and sting exposed skin.

entries.clue: Weary about doctor’s tone of voice (6)

indicatorNotes.about: About can mean around, so TIRE goes round MB.

blocks.note: MB = Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor

annotation.surface: A tired doctor with a particular manner of speaking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Weary' reads as an adjective describing the doctor; it is the verb TIRE.
annotation.definitionFit: A musical term: the distinctive colour of a sound that lets you tell one singer or instrument from another.

entries.clue: Beast roaming two thirds of Oregon (4)

indicatorNotes.roaming: Something roaming wanders from its place, so the letters move into a new order.
indicatorNotes.two thirds of: Two thirds of a six-letter word is four letters, so keep OREG and drop GON.

blocks.note: the first four of OREGON's six letters

annotation.surface: A monster wandering across much of an American state.
annotation.walkthrough: Oregon is a US state, which makes the roaming beast sound like a bear or bigfoot.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: the man-eating giant of fairy tales is a monstrous creature.

entries.clue: State of stagnation far from new in barrels of oil? (8)

indicatorNotes.in: Something put in barrels sits inside them, so OLD goes inside DRUMS.

annotation.surface: An economy stuck in a slump, with old oil barrels lying about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barrels of oil' sounds like the oil price; it just means oil drums.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from sailing: the windless equatorial calm where ships sat becalmed, now any spell of inactivity or low spirits.

entries.clue: Flirtation from each and every one during ball (9)

indicatorNotes.during: What happens during an event falls within it, so ALL I goes inside DANCE.

annotation.surface: Everyone at the ball is flirting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Each and every one' reads as a single phrase; split it into ALL and the numeral I.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a casual romantic toying or brief affair not taken seriously.

entries.clue: Who breaks things left behind London museum? (6)

indicatorNotes.behind: What is behind something comes after it, so L follows the museum.

blocks.note: the V&A, the Victoria and Albert Museum, with & written as AND

annotation.surface: Someone who wrecks things and leaves them behind at a London museum.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left behind' reads as abandoned; it is L placed after the museum. The V&A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: someone who deliberately smashes or defaces property, named after the tribe that sacked Rome.

entries.clue: Something less than a major route overseas (6)

annotation.definition: Something less than a major route

blocks.clueFragment: Something less than a major route
blocks.note: British roads are graded A (major) then B (minor), so read the answer as three parts: a single letter, a letter grade, then a word for route

annotation.surface: A minor road abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: British roads are graded: A roads are major routes, B roads lesser ones, so 'a B road' is something less than a major route.
annotation.definitionFit: Read as A B-ROAD it names a minor British road; as one word it means in a foreign country.

entries.clue: Car park associated with house? (6)

blocks.note: the British name for a station wagon, a long car with a rear door
the grounds of a country house

annotation.surface: Parking a car next to a house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Car park' looks like one thing; split it, and each half starts a definition. An estate is the British name for a station wagon.
annotation.definitionFit: British usage for a station wagon, and also the grounds and parkland belonging to a country mansion.

entries.clue: Country’s queen formerly travelling by rail? (7)

indicatorNotes.travelling by: A passenger travelling by train rides inside it, so ER goes inside TRAIN.

blocks.note: ER = Elizabeth Regina, the late queen
going by rail means taking the train

annotation.surface: A former queen touring her kingdom by train.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country' is not a nation here but land, as in rough country.
annotation.definitionFit: Country in the landscape sense, as in hill country: a stretch of land and its physical features.

entries.clue: To an extent, any fitter people running round will get trim (8)

indicatorNotes.To an extent: Something true to an extent is only partly true, so only part of the words is used.
indicatorNotes.running round: Running round means turning back the other way, so the letters are read backwards.

blocks.note: anY FITTER People, then read backwards

annotation.surface: Joggers who are fitter will slim down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trim' looks like an adjective for fit runners; it is the verb, to decorate.
annotation.definitionFit: Trim as a verb means adorn, as when you trim a hat with ribbon or a tree with baubles.

entries.clue: Opening of the grass flower (5)

indicatorNotes.Opening of: The opening of something is where it starts, so take the first letter of 'the'.

blocks.note: grass and weed are both slang for cannabis

annotation.surface: A grass that comes into flower.
annotation.walkthrough: A flower is something that flows: a river. The Tweed runs along the border of England and Scotland.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword-only sense: flower means something that flows, a river, and the Tweed is a Scottish border river.

entries.clue: Regretting missing university’s call (4)

indicatorNotes.missing: Something missing is absent, so U is taken out of the word.

annotation.surface: A student regrets missing the call from their university.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Missing' seems to be about missing a phone call, but it removes U.
annotation.definitionFit: British usage: to phone someone, from the bell that sounds on the other end.

entries.clue: Wants what Able Baker does in radio comms? (5)

indicatorNotes.in radio comms: Over the radio a word is heard, never seen, so only its sound counts.

annotation.surface: Signallers asking what 'Able Baker' means in the old radio alphabet.
annotation.walkthrough: Able and Baker were the old radio code words for A and B, so the clue seems to spell letters. Instead 'Able' just means capable: a good baker kneads.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what someone lacks and requires, as in 'wants for nothing'.

entries.clue: Time to maintain new pub (6)

blocks.note: to aver is to maintain, to insist something is true

annotation.surface: Time to keep a new pub going.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maintain' reads as upkeep; here it means to assert, AVER.
annotation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned synonym: an inn or bar selling beer and wine to drinkers.

entries.clue: Stones, v. small or v. large possibly (6)

indicatorNotes.possibly: Possibly signals one arrangement among many that could be, so the letters are reordered.

annotation.surface: Grading stones as very small or very large.
annotation.walkthrough: 'v. small or v. large' looks like a pair of size grades; the first half belongs to the definition and the second is the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: loose tiny pebbles used for paths and driveways.

entries.clue: Brilliant cut and mounted? (3)

blocks.note: the surface wants an adjective of praise; in fact a brilliant is a diamond with many facets
sounds like a sequence of wounds or a horse ride; it is what a jeweller does to the stone

annotation.surface: Something excellent being cut and then climbed on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brilliant' looks like an adjective of praise; it is a noun, a many-faceted diamond, which is cut and then set in a mount.
annotation.definitionFit: A faceted diamond, shaped and set in a ring, is a precious stone ready to wear.

entries.clue: Inattention getting sack, perhaps, around a pit (10)

indicatorNotes.around: What goes around something encircles it, so DRESS wraps round A MINE.

blocks.note: a sack dress is a loose, shapeless dress

annotation.surface: A miner not paying attention gets the sack.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Getting sack' suggests being fired for not paying attention; 'perhaps' marks a sack as one example of a dress.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a drifting, head-in-the-clouds state where the mind wanders from the task.
